en: Regarding the sixth section, "The Original Text of the Sūtra Commentary," composed by the Śramaṇa Ji: The former Master Zun stated, "The twenty-eight chapters are divided into two parts:
the first chapter clarifies the introduction to the Tathāgata’s manifestation of transformation, while the remainder..."

The twenty-seven chapters distinguish its authentic transformation, while the "Introduction Chapter" (Prastāvanā-parivarta) sets forth its initial origins; the authentic transformation clarifies its benefits, for from beginning to end, throughout until the conclusion of the sutra, there is benefit in every respect.
Master Jizang said:

"The first chapter is named the Introductory Section (Nidāna). The subsequent fifteen chapters and a half constitute the Main Body (Saddharma), extending from the beginning of the 'Chapter on the Distinction of Merit' up to the end of the verses on comparative measurement, because these clarify the provisional and real aspects of the vehicle, as well as the provisional and real aspects of the body, thereby constituting the Main Body."
Śāriputra’s three requests clarify the provisional and ultimate aspects of the vehicle;

Maitreya’s three requests clarify the provisional and ultimate aspects of the body. In the second verse of that [chapter], the prose section explains that the merit of hearing this lifespan and attaining faith and understanding is immeasurable; furthermore, the eleven chapters that follow constitute the section on the propagation of the teaching.
The Dharma Master Jing said:

"The first chapter is named the Introductory Section; the next nineteen chapters are named the Main Body; and the eight chapters following the 'Chapter on Supernatural Powers' are named the Dissemination."
Although this classification exists, it does not explain the reasons for it.
Now, two interpretations are offered:

first, one chapter is named the Introductory Section (Nidāna); second, eight chapters are named the Main Body (Śarīra). This is because the One Vehicle is correctly expounded and the predictions are bestowed upon those of the three faculties; the primary purpose has been fulfilled as all have already obtained benefit, and they are thereby transformed so that the Two Vehicles may emerge from the turbid waters.
This sutra states below:

"In this present sutra, only the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) is taught; yet in the past, before the bodhisattvas, the Buddha disparaged the śrāvakas who delight in inferior teachings. However, the Buddha has in truth always used the Mahāyāna to transform and teach."

Furthermore, in the "Devadatta Chapter," it says: "The Bodhisattva Jñānakośa addressed the Buddha Prabhūtaratna, requesting that he return to his original land. Thus we know that only when the task was completed did he request his return; it is therefore clear that the locus where the One Vehicle is taught is precisely the central theme of the sutra.

If it were the case that only those passages where benefit is obtained without the explicit teaching of the One Vehicle (ekayāna) constitute the main body of the teaching (samyak-siddhānta), then the passage in the "Universal Worthy Chapter" (*Samantabhadra-parivarta*)—wherein immeasurable bodhisattvas attain dharanis and bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in three thousandfold world-systems practice the path of Universal Worthy—would also have to be considered part of the main body of the teaching, since they too obtain benefit without the explicit teaching of the One Vehicle.
If that were so, then the ancient masters would have been our guides.
Furthermore, since the matter was not yet concluded, why did Zhizhi (Zhiji) request to return midway?

Alternatively, one might consider the first half of eight chapters, including the "Dharma Master" chapter, as the true orthodox teaching (*samyak-nītārtha*), because at the beginning of the "Dharma Master" chapter, those present—both ordinary and holy—who had seen, heard, or rejoiced in the teaching were granted the prediction of Bodhi.

In the "Dhāraṇī Chapter," although the prediction for the bhikṣuṇīs seated before him was bestowed, it was because they requested that the Buddha bestow predictions upon those who uphold the sūtra that he granted them; furthermore, he stated that he had already bestowed predictions on all previously and would no longer speak of the One Vehicle. Therefore, this is not the primary teaching.
The remaining nineteen chapters are collectively termed the "Circulation" section, as they praise, certify, receive the mandate, and entrust the teaching for its dissemination.

Alternatively, the initial introduction is no different from what was previously described; from the "Expedient Means" chapter down to the "Encouragement of Universal Worthy" chapter, these twelve chapters clarify the realm of the One Vehicle. The two chapters, "Peaceful Practices" and "Emergence from the Earth," clarify the practice of the One Vehicle. From the "Tathāgata’s Life Span" chapter down to the "Never-Disparaging" chapter, these five chapters together explain the fruit of the One Vehicle.

By expounding on the objective realm (*viṣaya*), he causes them to know the provisional and the real (*neyārtha* and *nītārtha*) of the vehicles, and exhorts them to abandon the provisional and adopt the real;

upon awakening to this, the śrāvakas subsequently receive their predictions (*vyākaraṇa*). By expounding on practice (*caryā*), he causes them to know the right and wrong of the causes, and exhorts them to study what is right and eliminate what is wrong; through this, the learners emerge from the earth. By expounding on the fruit (*phala*), he causes them to know the true and emanated nature of the body, as well as the causes and fruits of realization; he exhorts them to recognize the emanated and seek realization of the true, gradually attaining the supreme virtues of both the causal and fruitional stages; upon knowing this, the bodhisattvas subsequently realize the path, fully manifesting the supreme virtues accomplished by cause and fruit.

From the "Chapter on Supernatural Powers" (*Ṛddhi-parivarta*) onwards, all sections are designated as the "Circulation, Manifestation of Signs, and Entrustment," because they involve receiving the mandate and putting it into practice; the reasons for these designations will all be explained below.

The treatise states that the "Introductory Chapter" (*Nidāna-parivarta*) possesses seven kinds of accomplishments (*siddhi*). "Accomplishment" carries the meaning of being fully endowed and perfected; this is intended to clarify that the introduction is complete with seven meanings, as other sūtras lack such perfection in these seven points.

First, the accomplishment of the introductory section (*nidāna*): it is first described because it possesses the complete causes for universal penetration; the "City Mountain" (*śaila-pura*) is called the "introductory section" because its perfection symbolizes its superiority over others, though in reality all seven [sections] constitute the introduction.

The accomplishment of the two assemblies is indicated by the section beginning with "with a great assembly of bhikṣus. This consists of: first, the number; second, the conduct; third, the inclusion of meritorious qualities; and fourth, the perfection of abiding in accordance with the Dharma through majestic deportment, as it excels other sūtras.

When the Tathāgata was about to preach the Dharma, he reached the stage of fulfillment; the section beginning with "for the sake of the bodhisattvas, he preached the Mahāyāna sūtras" follows this. First, he preached the *Anantārthasūtra*, which possesses seventeen titles, as it is superior to other sūtras.

Fourth is the accomplishment of abiding in a posture that accords with the Dharma as the basis for teaching; this is indicated by the passage beginning, "After the Buddha had spoken this sutra, he sat cross-legged.

This is because these three types of phenomena—reliance on meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*), and the sentient-being-world (*sattva-loka*)—are not found in other sūtras.

The fifth is the accomplishment of the causal basis for the teaching, which begins with the passage "At that time, the Buddha emitted light from between his eyebrows. This is because one perceives such matters as the illuminating power, the object illuminated, and the act of illumination, thereby giving rise to a sense of rare wonder—a phenomenon not found in other sūtras.

Regarding the accomplishment of the six classes of sentient beings desiring to hear the Dharma in their presence, the section beginning with "At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva had this thought" follows; although he questions only one person, many people develop a sense of rare wonder at the desire to hear [the teaching], which does not occur in other sutras.

Seventh, Mañjuśrī’s answer was accomplished because, through the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*), he directly perceived the characteristics of causes and effects from the past; thus, the ten matters were accomplished as if appearing before his eyes, enabling him to provide the answer. This is not the case in other sūtras.

The seven [sections] are divided into two parts: the first two constitute the general introduction (*sādhāraṇa-nidāna*), and the latter five constitute the specific introduction (*asādhāraṇa-nidāna*).

The general introduction has five components: (1) a general manifestation of what was heard; (2) the time when the teaching was spoken; (3) the teacher who spoke it; (4) the place where those to be converted were gathered; and (5) the capacity of the audience to whom it was addressed. When these are combined with the entry into the assembly, the introduction consists of four parts; "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) constitutes the first, as it is intended to inspire faith by manifesting that which was personally heard.
The root treatise mentions only two introductory accomplishments:
first, the city; second, the mountain.
These two locations are superior and distinct from those in other sūtras, which is why they are specifically mentioned.

Regarding the phrase "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*), it is no different from other sūtras; although this formula is present in all sūtras, its excellence is not specifically distinguished [in others]. This [formula] is analyzed through three gates:
first, the reason for its being spoken; second, the reason for its establishment; and third, the formal explanation of its text.

Regarding the reason for this teaching, as explained in the *Mahāśālopama-sūtra* and other scriptures concerning its original causes: when the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he commanded that those with doubts should ask questions. At that time, Upāli and Anuruddha instructed Ānanda to inquire about four matters: first, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, whom should the bhikṣus take as their teacher?
second, upon what should they rely for their dwelling? third, how should bhikṣus of evil character be disciplined? and fourth, what words should be placed at the beginning of all sūtras?
The Buddha said:
"After my parinirvāṇa, take the Prātimokṣa as your great teacher; act in accordance with the precepts;
dwell by means of the four foundations of mindfulness, establishing your mind therein."

An evil-natured bhikṣu is to be disciplined through *brahmadanda*; because *brahmadanda* is characterized by silence, one should not strike or revile him, but rather exclude him through silent ostracism;
furthermore, the words "Thus have I heard" and so forth should be placed at the beginning of all sūtras.
Later, when Ānanda performed the compilation, he followed the Buddha’s teachings; he extensively recounted the origins [of the teachings] exactly as they are set forth in the sūtras.
The reason for establishing [the canon] was to cause sentient beings to give rise to faith and compliance.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"'Thus have I heard' gives rise to faith;
'faithfully accepting and practicing' gives rise to wisdom."

Faith is that which enables entry, while wisdom is that which enables transcendence; faith is the primary foundation for entering the Dharma, and wisdom is the profound art of ultimate realization. When faith exists, the principles of what is taught accord with reality; when they accord, the way of teacher and disciple is established. Because of faith, all the teachings spoken can be followed in accordance with truth; because of this accordance, the relationship between speaker and listener, and teacher and disciple, is formed.
Regarding this faith, there are briefly ten explanations:

first, it is the primary cause for proceeding toward the ultimate fruit; according to scriptures such as the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*, it is the primary cause for proceeding toward the stages of the noble ones (*ārya*), and thus the forty minds take faith as their foremost.

To initially generate the great bodhicitta, one must possess ten virtues and give rise to three sublime contemplations. The great bodhicitta takes roots of goodness as its essence, virtuous friends as its condition, and non-retrogression as its impetus.
The roots of goodness consist of faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"Through the power of pure supremacy, with a firm mind and superior progress, this is called the Bodhisattva’s initial cultivation over three incalculable great eons."

The gradual basis for entering the principle of the Two Truths is such that all treatises state that one who is about to enter the stage of the Noble Ones possesses the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) and the power of faith (*śraddhābala*).
Because the faculty of faith exists, all manner of wholesome qualities arise therefrom;
because the power of faith exists, the four Māras cannot subdue them. For this reason, this sutra first and foremost causes faith to arise.

The three supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) are the realization of the sublime truth and purity; they enable one to transcend the evil realms and abandon the causes of low birth and poverty. Thus, having entered the state of a noble one (*ārya*), one realizes the four unshakable faiths (*aveṇikaśraddhā*): by faith in the Triple Gem, one can transcend the evil realms; and by faith in the precepts, one abandons the causes of low birth and poverty. Therefore, the treatise also speaks of the "clear observation through faith" (*śraddhābhisamaya*).

Fourth is the reliance on the joy of the supreme virtue. The *Vibhāṣā* states that faith is the hand that partakes of the excellence of the flavor of the Dharma. One who studies the Buddha-dharma is like a great nāga-elephant: taking faith as its hand, relinquishment as its tusks, mindfulness as its neck, and wisdom as its head, it carries and gathers all wholesome dharmas upon its two shoulders.
The elephant uses its trunk as its hand for drinking and eating; likewise, those who study the Buddha-dharma first give rise to faith.

It is the primordial matrix of the five spiritual faculties and the seven riches of the noble ones. Because it is the primary source of the wealth of the Dharma, the student is like a great merchant who first seeks the precious jewels of the Dharma and, through the teaching, acquires the noble riches; therefore, one first gives rise to faith.
The *Xianyang lun* states:
"The seven noble riches are faith, ethical discipline, learning, relinquishment, wisdom, shame, and dread of blame; faith is the first among them."
"The six roots of goodness are the auspicious path because they are the foundation of wholesome dharmas.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:

"Entering into all wholesome dharmas has desire as its root; it is produced by attention (*manasikāra*), gathered by contact (*sparśa*), sustained by feeling (*vedanā*), dominated by concentration (*samādhi*), supreme in wisdom (*prajñā*), firm in liberation (*vimukti*), and culminates in renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa*)."

Desire is fundamental because it gives rise to aspiration; attention is fundamental because it repeatedly arouses mental alertness; contact is fundamental because it brings about the gathering and harmony of the mind and mental factors in response to superior conditions; feeling is fundamental because it draws in and sustains what is experienced within the mind; concentration is fundamental because it is the predominant factor for the subtle stilling of the mind; wisdom is fundamental because it is the most excellent means for discerning between good and evil; liberation is fundamental because it is the firm cessation of entanglements and bonds; and renunciation is fundamental because it constitutes the final stage of the path to awakening.
Since faith is the basis for desire, it is made to arise first.
It is the manual for opening the door of the sevenfold arousal of the faculties and the hand that receives the teaching; as the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* says:
"It pulls sentient beings out from the mire of birth and death."

Furthermore, the subsequent exposition of the orthodox teaching is the hand of the Buddha, while the introduction that inspires faith is the hand of sentient beings; thus, by joining these two hands, one emerges from the mud.
Moreover, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"If a person has hands, they may take whatever they desire upon reaching a mountain of jewels; yet if they have no hands, they will come away empty-handed with nothing gained."

Those with faith enter the Jewel Mountain of the Buddha and attain the fruits of the various paths; yet, if one lacks faith, even if they understand the literal meaning of the texts, they will gain nothing at all.
The clear pearl of the eightfold tranquil waters purifies the mind; as the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"Faith is like a water-clearing pearl that can purify turbid water," for it can remedy the natural turbidity of a lack of faith.
The establishment of a reputation is an excellent resource for the Way. Confucius said:

"Of the three—military force, food, and good faith—one must not abandon good faith. From ancient times until now, all have died; yet no one can stand without good faith. It would be like a large carriage without its crossbar (ni) or a small carriage without its yoke-socket (yu); if a person lacks good faith, one does not know how they could function."
Regarding these ten points of sincere and noble expectations, the *Spring and Autumn Annals* states:

"If there is sincere faith, then even the grasses from mountain ravines and marshes, or vegetables such as duckweed, water-moss, floating pondweed, and submerged algae, may be offered to the spirits and presented to the dukes and kings; how much more so when a gentleman establishes the good faith between two states."

Regarding these ten meanings herein, the first eight rely on the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and the latter two rely on the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Therefore, the sūtra begins with "Thus" (*evam*), indicating that the meaning of the sūtra was heard directly from the Buddha and is free from the faults of addition or omission; this is for the purpose of causing sentient beings to give rise to a mind of faith and joy, so that they may practice and train accordingly.
To provide a formal commentary on this passage, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"The phrase 'thus' (evam) functions according to four meanings. First, it relies on analogy;

as when it is said, 'Such wealth and nobility are like those of Vaiśravaṇa,' so too, the Dharma that has been transmitted and heard is exactly as the Buddha taught, certainly without any difference, and is certainly a cause for the skillful means of benefit and happiness, or the spoken words and phrases are exactly as I previously heard them."

Second, regarding reliance on instruction: as it is said, "You should read and recite the sūtras and śāstras in this manner. Here, "in this manner" refers, distantly, to the instruction of the Buddha, and proximately, to the instruction of those who transmit the Dharma;
or it may be addressed to the assembled multitude, saying, "In this manner, you should listen to what I have heard in the past."
Third, based on the question-and-answer format:
it refers to someone asking, "Did you hear what you are about to say in the past?
Therefore, one answers, "Thus have I heard."
Fourth, regarding the authorization:
as it is said, "I shall think thus for you, act thus for you, and speak thus for you. This refers to when the assembly of bodhisattvas collectively requested at the time of the compilation:
"You should speak exactly as you have heard."
The Bodhisattva who transmits the Dharma then granted his permission, saying:
"It shall be spoken thus, exactly as I have heard it;
or one may speak with confidence, saying:"
This matter is thus; that is to say, such is the Dharma as I have heard in the past, and this matter is exactly so. Up to this point, it shall be explained with certainty and without any variation.
For these four reasons, the phrase "Thus have I heard" (evam mayā śrutam) is placed at the beginning of every sutra.
The Tripitaka Master Paramārtha stated:

"The *Sūkṣma-vinaya* clarifies that when Ānanda ascended the seat to compile the Dharma-piṭaka, his body was endowed with all the marks and signs like those of the Buddhas; when he descended from the seat, he returned to his original form. The *Khan-chi-tsang-chuan* (Record of the Compilation of the Piṭaka) also makes this same statement."
Sentient beings have three doubts:

first, they doubt that the Buddha’s great compassion has arisen from nirvana to further preach the wondrous Dharma; second, they doubt that another Buddha has come from another direction to dwell here and preach the Dharma; third, they doubt that Ānanda has transformed his body to become a Buddha and is preaching the Dharma for the assembly.

I now clarify that the Dharma thus taught was personally heard by me while attending the Buddha in the past; it is not the case that the Buddha has arisen anew, nor that a Buddha from another direction has arrived, nor that he has attained Buddhahood through the transformation of his body.
To eliminate this doubt, the sutra begins with the words, "Thus have I heard.
The circumstances of the compilation are as explained in the section on the *Tripiṭaka*.
The *Commentary on the Lotus Sutra* (*Fahua zhuyi*) states:
"Such is the auspicious omen of resonance; it receives its name according to the compliance with capacities, and thus there is nothing that does not establish its designation.

Sentient beings take 'thusness' (non-fault) as their stimulus, and the Tathāgata provides the response by complying with their capacities. Since the transmitters of the sutras wish to reveal that the teaching arises from this resonance, they utter the words, 'Thus'."
The *Commentary on the Immeasurable Meanings* states:
"When the Perfected One preaches the Dharma, he does so solely to manifest suchness (*tathatā*). Since only suchness is what is correct, he says 'Thus' (*evam*)."
Master Bao said:
"That which is free from the five types of slander is called 'thus' (*tathā*).
Regarding the first phrase, 'thus,' this sutra is free from the slander of superimposition (*samāropa*) that clings to existence."
The second phrase: thus, this sūtra is free from the clinging that constitutes the denial of existence (apavāda).
The third phrase: thus, this sūtra is free from the clinging that constitutes the contradictory denial of both existence and non-existence.
The fourth phrase: thus, this sutra is free from the foolish slander of clinging to the notions of neither existence nor non-existence.
The fifth phrase: thus, this sutra is free from the conceptual proliferation of slander clinging to the notion of neither non-existence nor non-non-existence.
Guangzhai said:
"'Thus' serves as a preface to introduce the portion being transmitted before what was heard;
it indicates that this particular scripture was personally heard by me from the Buddha, thereby establishing the precedent for the phrase 'I have heard.'"
Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty said:
"The meaning of 'evam' (thus) is that because this is what the Buddha has taught, it is called 'evam'.
The Tripiṭaka Master Dīrghakarṇa said:
“There are three aspects to this:
first, with respect to the Buddha, the Buddhas of the three periods of time all teach without difference, which is called ‘Suchness’ (*tathatā*); because they teach in common, it is termed ‘Thus.

Second, with respect to the Dharma, the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena does not change from antiquity to the present, and is thus named ‘Suchness’; because one teaches for the sake of Suchness, it is termed ‘Thus.’”

Third, regarding the Sangha: because Ānanda heard and upheld the Buddha’s original teachings, and what he transmitted did not differ from them, it is called "Thus" (Tathā); because it is forever free from error and transgression, it is termed "Right" (Samyak).

Because it is spoken thus in common with others, it is consistent with reason and free from error; since what has been transmitted is not different [from other authentic sources], the sūtra is trustworthy.
Altogether, there are fifteen such explanations above.

Regarding the phrase "I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*), the Bodhisattva who transmits the Dharma refers to himself, stating that he personally heard this Dharma from the Buddha; therefore, it is called "I heard. This does not mean that the term "I" necessarily belongs to a single specific individual.
I maintain that the "self" refers to the conventional, provisional designation of the aggregates (*skandha*). However, there are three types of self:
first, the self erroneously clung to, which refers to the self arbitrarily imputed by non-Buddhists and others;
second, the conventionally designated self, which refers to the Great Nirvāṇa as bliss, purity, permanence, and self—so designated because it removes the perverse attachments of the two vehicles.
The "I" that circulates through the three periods of time refers to what is commonly transmitted in the world, such as Devadatta or Yajñadatta.

Now, those who transmit the Dharma conform to worldly convention by using the term "I" to refer to themselves; this differs from the former two cases and is precisely the "Great Self" that is actually selfless.
Question:

Since the Buddhas’ teaching of the Dharma is fundamentally intended to eliminate the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*), why do they not state "non-self" (*anātman*) but instead say "I have heard" (*evaṃ mayā śrutam*)?
Answer:
There are four reasons:

first, because it is easy to explain; for if one were to speak of "selflessness" (anātman) as applying to the aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu), one would need to know to whom this refers.
Second, because it accords with worldly convention.
Third, because it removes the fear of non-self: if there were no self, for whom would one practice and study?
Fourth, because there exist distinctions such as self and other, defilement and purity, cause and effect, and various activities, one speaks of a "self."
Question:
If that is so, why does he not mention his name but refer only to "I"?
Answer:
There are three meanings:

first, it demonstrates that one does not deviate from worldly convention; for although the fundamental principle reveals the ultimate truth, the language does not deviate from the conventional, and although the underlying logic reveals the subtle, the expression does not become coarse, because one wishes to demonstrate that the ultimate truth is not separate from the conventional.
The second, "ātman," carries the meaning of a sovereign or independent master.
The *Saṃyuktāgama* states:
"There are three Ānandas:..."
First is Ānanda, translated as "Joyful," who upholds the Śrāvaka-piṭaka;
second is Ānandabhadra, translated as "Virtuous Joy," who upholds the Pratyekabuddha-piṭaka;
third is Ānandakara, translated as "Ocean of Joy," who upholds the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
However, they are but a single person whose names differ according to their respective virtues.

For this reason, Ānanda—being one who has heard much, who retains what he has heard, and whose hearing has been accumulated—is fully equipped with the three types of wisdom and maintains both the letter and the meaning; he possesses sovereign mastery over the total retention (*dhāraṇī*) of the teachings of the Tripiṭaka. While it would accord with correct principle to call him by that name, he does not possess the sense of having attained mastery over all phenomena.
For this reason, I do not address Ānanda as "I.
Thirdly, "I" signifies intimacy; in common worldly parlance, one says "I see" or "I hear," which is taken as direct personal testimony.

If it were said that "Ānanda heard," it might imply he did not hear it directly from the Buddha but received it through transmission from another; now, to demonstrate that he heard it directly from the World-Honored One’s own speech and was not merely repeating hearsay—and thus to shatter the web of doubt held by others—it is stated simply as "I heard" rather than by name.
"Hearing" refers to the ear-faculty giving rise to consciousness to listen to and receive what is spoken.
Now, setting aside the specific faculty of the ear and adopting a general designation for the self, it is said: "I heard."

Although "hearing" is designated as such only when there is a conjunction of the sense organ, consciousness, mental factors, and the object—based on the Mahāyāna perspective—the sense organ is superior to consciousness and the other factors in five respects; therefore, the sense organ alone is named "hearing."
The five meanings of the sense-faculties (*indriya*) are: basis, origination, belonging, assistance, and being like a faculty.

Regarding "being like a faculty": just as the clarity or dullness of the faculty determines the clarity or dullness of consciousness, if one merely hears a sound, it may pertain only to the ear; yet once it takes up names and meanings, it then resides within the mind.
Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Hearing refers to inference (*anumāna*).

As for why the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*) is called "hearing": it is because one directly hears sound, which serves as a gateway for the mental faculty (*manas*), and only then does the mind hear; since these two serve as gateways, the resulting habitual impressions (*vāsanā*) reside in the aggregate (*sāmānya*). Because that which is accomplished based on hearing is collectively termed "hearing," the specific faculties of the ear and mind are set aside, and the aggregate is referred to as "I have heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*).
Question:
Since Ānanda at that time personally saw, perceived, and understood what the Buddha had spoken, why did he say only "I have heard" (*śruta*) and not "I have seen" (*dṛṣṭa*) and so forth?
Answer:
There are three reasons:
first, to realize the profound principle, one must first hear the Dharma; for names and so forth express meaning, whereas form and so forth do not.
Second, in this realm, the Buddha’s work is accomplished through sound, because names and so forth exist with sound as their basis.
Third, the aspiration to realize bodhi requires the hearing-perfuming (*śruta-vāsanā*), for it is through the hearing-perfuming that one achieves the supramundane.
For this reason, the beginning of this sutra does not mention "seeing, perceiving, or knowing," but speaks only of "I have heard.

In reality, at that time, one did indeed see the Buddha preaching; furthermore, in other buddha-fields, the Buddha’s work is performed through light and so forth, which can be described as "seeing" and so on—one should apply such distinctions to this meaning.
Question:
Is it that one says "I am able to hear" when the Buddha preaches the Dharma, or is it that one says "I hear" even when the Buddha does not preach?
Answer:
There are two interpretations.
First, Nāgasena and others state:
"The Buddha possesses only three qualities, namely: great concentration, wisdom, and compassion."

For a long time, he has been free from conceptual proliferation and has never preached the Dharma; yet, through the power of the Buddha’s compassion and the conditions of his original vows, the aspects of words and meanings arise within the consciousness of sentient beings. Although these aspects of words and meanings arise primarily by relying on the power of one's own roots of goodness, they are called "the Buddha’s preaching" because of their dominant condition. Because they arise through the power of the auditory faculty and one's own mental transformation, they are termed "I have heard," which constitutes their essential nature.
Therefore, Wuxing said:

"In accordance with the eight periods [of the day], whether what is heard appears on the consciousness as direct or indirect speech, it manifests through accumulation, taking this as its essential nature."
He raises an objection himself, saying:
"If that is so, how can a bodhisattva be able to teach?
At the beginning of that treatise, it says:

“O Bhagavat, because a bodhisattva who has already been able to skillfully enter the Mahāyāna, in order to manifest the greatness of the essence of the Mahāyāna, has spoken the ‘Chapter on the Compendium of the Mahāyāna,’ this objection is raised.”
The treatise further answers itself:

"This was said because of his superior power (*adhipati-bala*); for example, by the superior power of the gods and others, one may obtain treatises, mantras, and so forth within a dream. Thus, a sutra also says:
'From the initial attainment of enlightenment until reaching nirvana, in the interval between these two, not a single word was spoken.'"
"Just as when a mother's teeth or fingers [are injured], the child cries out for relief.
Second, Bandhuprabha and others say:

"The Buddha’s body possesses the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus); it is called 'free from conceptual proliferation' (niṣprapañca) because it is free from discursive discrimination. But would it not also be called 'free from conceptual proliferation' when teaching the Dharma?"

This means that through the power of the roots of goodness, vows, and conditions of those who are fit to hear, the aspects of words and meanings arise within the consciousness of the Tathāgata. These aspects of words and meanings are produced by the Buddha’s own roots of goodness for the benefit of others and are thus called "the Buddha’s teaching. Although those who hear do not directly perceive them within their own consciousness, these aspects appear clearly and distinctly as if they were present; therefore, it is said, "I have heard."
Vasubandhu states:

"This means that because of the differentiation of consciousness within one continuum, it causes a differentiated consciousness to arise in another continuum, since they serve as mutual dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for one another."
As this sutra states:

"The Dharma I have taught is like the leaves in my hand; the Dharma I have not yet taught is like the leaves in the forest. This is because, like a mani jewel or a celestial drum, it performs its function without volition.
Regarding this, two interpretations follow their respective texts, providing alternating explanations.

One should understand that the statement "Thus have I heard" is intended to avoid the faults of addition, subtraction, or deviation from the original; that is, it indicates: "I heard this Dharma directly from the Buddha, not through successive transmission from others."

Those who hear [this] possess the capacity [for realization]; whatever they hear is entirely free from the faults of exaggeration (*samāropa*), underestimation (*apavāda*), and deviation (*anyathātva*). This is not like the case of the foolish, who lack such capacity and cannot avoid these faults of exaggeration, underestimation, and deviation when hearing things.

When the compilers of the Dharma transmitted the Buddha’s teachings, they uttered these words at the outset of the teaching in order to inspire reverence, faith, and acceptance among sentient beings: "Such a Dharma as this, I have heard from the Buddha. Thus, the words and their meanings are definitive and free from addition or subtraction. Therefore, those who hear it should listen correctly, reflect upon it according to reason, and diligently practice and study it.
Regarding the sūtra’s phrase “at one time,” the commentary states:
This second [section] explains the temporal period of the teaching.
This has two meanings:

first, when the Dharma King initiates his transformation and the receptive vessels have all assembled, the entire period from the beginning of the preaching until its conclusion is collectively termed "one time.

Second, because the speaker and the listeners meet together and there is no distinction in the temporal division, it is called "one time"; for there is likewise no distinction in time between the stimulus of the receptive capacity and the response of the transformative manifestation.
Regarding the initial explanation that "one time" (*ekakṣaṇa*) refers to a continuous succession without interruption during speaking and listening, it is ultimately a conventional designation.

There are two interpretations of this: First, regarding the time according to principle (*yukti-kāla*): although both the speaker and the listener exist only in the present, the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) and all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) arise and perish moment by moment. Within these very present phenomena, there is the sense of one moment responding to a preceding one and inducing a succeeding one. That which is responded to is conventionally designated as "past," and that which is induced is conventionally designated as "future. In relation to these two, the current state is called "present. These past and future periods are both provisionally established upon the present phenomena themselves. Thus, the five aggregates and all phenomena of the speaker and listener arise and perish moment by moment in a continuous succession; when this entire process is finalized, the three times are provisionally established, and the whole is collectively termed "one time. This does not refer to a single moment of arising and perishing.

Second, regarding the time of "consciousness-only": for both the speaker and the listener, it arises as the transformation of the three temporal phases upon their cognitive minds. In reality, these are present; however, according to the limitations of the mind, they transform into durations of varying length, and when the sequence of events is completed, they are collectively termed "one period."
Just as what is seen in a dream is said to involve many births, yet upon waking one realizes it is merely mind with no real objects at all;

so too is the transformation of the listener’s mind regarding the three periods of time. It is solely an object of the mental faculty, belonging to the formations dissociated from thought (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), and is subsumed within the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) and the dharma-base (*dharmāyatana*).

Regarding this term "at one time" (*ekasmin samaye*): first, it is not necessarily restricted to a single *kṣaṇa*; second, it is not necessarily restricted to a single continuous sequence; third, it is not necessarily restricted to four periods, six periods, eight periods, twelve periods, and so forth; fourth, it is not necessarily restricted to a specific number of years or seasons following the attainment of enlightenment. Rather, it refers to the completion of the act of speaking and listening: when the listeners' faculties have matured and they are moved to request the Buddha's teaching, and the speaker, out of compassion, speaks in accordance with their capacity; the entire process of this teaching and listening is collectively termed "at one time."

Regarding the statement that "the indefinite [duration] is measured in moments (*kṣaṇa*) and so forth": the capacities of those who listen to the Dharma may be dull; thus, although the time of speaking is short, the time for understanding through listening is long. Or, the speaker may speak for a long time and the listener likewise remains for a long duration, such that one cannot even understand it within a single moment. Therefore, it is not merely a matter of a single moment.

Furthermore, it is not restricted to a continuous sequence because the speaker, having attained *dhāraṇī*, can fully comprehend the meaning of all [words] through the expression of a single syllable; or the listener, having attained pure hearing and mental faculty, can understand everything upon hearing a single syllable. Therefore, it is not a continuous sequence.

Because the faculties of the listeners in a single assembly vary—some being sharp and others dull—the Tathāgata’s supernatural power may either extend a brief moment into a long kalpa or condense many kalpas into a brief moment; since this is not fixed, it is generally described as "at one time" (*ekasmin samaye*) based on the completion of both the teaching and the listening.

Furthermore, it is not fixed to four periods, six periods, eight periods, or twelve periods; for a single day or month, the sun illuminates the four continents, yet the lengths [of days], the warmth and cold, the proximity and distance, and the divisions of day and night vary across different regions, as its activity always arises simultaneously over two continents.

Furthermore, excluding the various heavens above and below, these four seasons and eight periods do not exist; this scripture was intended for circulation in higher realms and various regions, as it would not have spread universally had it been taught according to the four seasons and so forth.

Furthermore, there is no fixed determination regarding the number of years or the specific seasons following the attainment of enlightenment, because the Buddha-bodies perceived by ordinary and noble beings of the three vehicles—whether as *saṃbhoga-kāya* or *nirmāṇa-kāya*—differ respectively in the length of their lifespans and the duration since their attainment of enlightenment.

Since this sūtra is intended for the common hearing of both ordinary beings and sages across the three vehicles, it does not specify the number of years that have passed since his attainment of enlightenment.
However, there are other sūtras that speak of such continuity; this very sūtra states below that "this Lotus Sūtra was preached for a full sixty minor kalpas," which refers to precisely this matter.
Some say there are four periods: the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states, "on the fifteenth day of the second month.

Some say there are six, eight, or twelve periods: the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says, "at the time of chewing a tooth-stick in the early morning"; the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says, "having finished eating, put away his robes and bowl, washed his feet, spread out his seat, and sat down at the time of midday"; the *Sūtra on the Superior Rebirth* says, "during the first watch of the night, he emitted light from his entire body"; and the *Sūtra of the Final Teachings* says, "during the middle watch of the night, it was silent and without sound."

Regarding those who speak of the number of years and seasons following the attainment of the Way, the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* states: "In the second seven-day period, within the Maṇiratnagarbha Hall of the palace of the King of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, he preached the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Furthermore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: "After reflecting upon this for three seven-day periods, he proceeded to Vārāṇasī to turn the wheel of the Four Noble Truths. Moreover, the *Anantamukha-sādhaka Sūtra* and other such texts state: "Since my attainment of the Way, more than forty years have passed," and so forth.

Although this explanation exists, it was spoken merely as a summary by those who heard, saw, and compiled the teachings according to the specific region where the transformation-land beings resided; it does not refer to the original title given at the time the Dharma was first preached. Therefore, in all cases, one should state "at one time" as a general introductory phrase.
Question:

Regarding the places [of rebirth], there are pure and impure ones; these are definitively taught according to the capacities of beings. Regarding the times, there are distinctions between ordinary persons and sages; why then should they not be explained separately?
Answer:

The locations described indicate purity or defilement, and purity or defilement can be definitively known; yet the durations of these teachings vary, being sometimes short and sometimes long, such that they cannot be standardized according to whether the audience is noble or ordinary. Within a single assembly, the capacities of those present may be sharp or dull; how, then, can one establish a fixed standard for long or short durations?
Therefore, while the location can be specified, the time is stated only in general terms as "at one time.
Regarding the word "Buddha" in the sutra,
the commentary says:
The third [section] explains the Teacher.
In Sanskrit he is called "Buddha," which is abbreviated here as "Fo" (Buddha);
he is the Lord of Wisdom, and in the language of Tang (Chinese) he is called "Juezhe" (the Awakened One).
Awakening has three meanings:
first, self-awakening, which surpasses ordinary beings, for ordinary beings do not awaken by themselves;
second, awakening others, which surpasses those of the Two Vehicles, for they do not awaken others.
Third, the perfection of the three types of awakening surpasses that of all bodhisattvas, for although bodhisattvas cultivate the two types of awakening, their practice is not yet complete.
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:

"Possessing both omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), he is able to awaken himself and awaken all sentient beings; like waking from a dream or like a lotus blooming, he is therefore called a Buddha."
The Omniscient One is able to awaken his own wisdom, like awakening from a dream.
He contemplates the wisdom of emptiness, the wisdom of reality, the wisdom of truth, and non-conceptual wisdom, just as they truly are.

In general terms, the attainment of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) through the severance of the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) is the awakening to the wisdom of sentient beings, like the blossoming of a lotus flower.

This consists of the wisdom regarding existence, the wisdom regarding phenomena, conventional wisdom, and subsequently attained wisdom; these constitute the "exhaustion of all that exists" (*yāvadbhāvikatā*).
Generally speaking, this is attained by severing the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

According to various Sanskrit manuscripts of the sūtras, the Master is consistently referred to as *Bhagavat*; this is because the Buddhist teachings maintain that this single term encompasses all his virtues.
However, the primary translators, intending to provide an abbreviation for the sake of generating wholesome roots according to local customs, used the title "Buddha."
Question:
Among these three bodies, which body does it subsume?
Answer:
According to the circumstances and according to the capacities, he manifests as a Transformation Buddha (nirmāṇakāya) in response to śrāvakas;
according to the texts and according to the vessels, he teaches the bodhisattvas as the Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya).
Since those who are moved differ in their faculties and dispositions, these manifestations respond accordingly, thus encompassing both the Reward and Transformation bodies.
The royal city and Vulture Peak are consumed by the fires at the end of the kalpa; when Śāriputra hears the sutra, he immediately becomes a Buddha—this is the Transformation Body (nirmāṇakāya).
My land is peaceful and secure, its lifespan is vast and long, and Mañjuśrī dwells within it—this is the Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya).
The manifested transformation body is not the true Buddha, nor is it the speaker of the Dharma; when its merit is traced back to its source, it is none other than the Dharmakāya.
Therefore, the *Mahāyānaguṇaparikīrtana Sūtra* abides in the treasury of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātugarbha) to clarify the teaching of the Dharmakāya.
The *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* and other such texts, which abide in the eighteen perfections of the King of Jewel Flowers (*Ratnapadma-rāja*), were spoken by the *saṃbhogakāya*.
The traces of this sūtra-king in the royal city were spoken by the *nirmāṇakāya*.
From the perspective of principle, they actually pertain to all three Buddhas, for they manifest their bodies in accordance with sentient beings and are not fixed as one.
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states that the three Buddha-bodies each preach the Dharma separately, yet all of them preach the Dharma.

Because of this, the elder Ghoṣila gave rise to the aspiration for enlightenment upon seeing [the Buddha] at three feet in height; five hundred Brahmins conceived faith upon seeing his body reduced to ashes; the Bodhisattva Anantagātra reached the limits of the upper realms and yet found it insufficient; while ordinary beings dwelling as Lesser Sages contemplated him at sixteen feet and found it inexhaustible.
Now, to manifest the excellence of the Principal Teacher’s teaching according to meditative concentration, the text first identifies the Teacher to inspire joy in the audience.
The Sūtra states: "He was dwelling at Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak Mountain."
The commentary states:
This is the fourth location for those to be converted.
"Dwelling" (*sthiti*) refers to both wandering for conversion and residing; "dwelling" carries the meaning of residing, wandering for conversion, and abiding in peace.
While his dwelling was in the mountains, his sphere of activity for teaching and transforming beings was within the city; it was here that the Buddha relied to travel and dwell in peace.

Based on this, the ancients interpreted the abodes of the Sages (ārya), Devas, Brahmas, and Buddhas; though the names of these "abodes" (vihāra) are the same, their meanings and implications are entirely distinct.

Regarding the points where the language is profound and the meaning is obscure, you have never applied your mind; as for the texts that equate names yet distinguish meanings, your citations are hollow and exaggerated—this is unacceptable.

In Sanskrit it is called Kuśāgrapura, which in the language of Tang means "City of Superior Kusa Grass. It is located at the very center of the kingdom of Magadha, the site where former kings of antiquity resided. Because superior and auspicious *kuśa* grass abounds there, it was named accordingly.

Surrounded on all four sides by lofty mountains as its outer wall, it has a narrow path leading west and a mountain gate opening to the north; it is long from east to west and narrow from south to north, with a circumference of over one hundred and fifty *li*. The inner palace and the sub-city have a circumference of forty *li*. *Karnikāra* trees line all the roads; their flowers possess an extraordinary fragrance and a color as brilliant as gold, such that in the month of late spring, the entire forest is golden.

Outside the north gate of the palace city is a stūpa; this is the place where Devadatta, acting as a close friend to King Ajātaśatru, released the intoxicated elephant Dhanapāla in an attempt to harm the Tathāgata, and where the Tathāgata produced five lions from the tips of his fingers, causing the intoxicated elephant to prostrate itself in submission.
To the northeast of this is another stūpa, marking the place where Śāriputra met the bhikṣu Aśvajit and attained the first fruit of the path.

Not far to the north of this is a large, deep pit; this is the site where Śrīgupta (translated here as Shengmi)—who attempted to harm the Buddha by means of a fire-pit and poisoned rice—prepared his trap.

Traveling fourteen or fifteen *li* northeast from the palace city, one arrives at Gṛdhrakūṭa Parvata; in the language of Tang, this means "Vulture Peak" and is also called "Vulture Terrace. It adjoins the southern slope of the northern mountain range, rising solitary and preeminent. Since vultures have made their home there, and its shape resembles a high terrace, the azure-green of the sky and the lushness of the vegetation reflect one another, creating a play of deep and light hues. More than fifty years after the Buddha attained enlightenment, he frequently resided on this mountain to extensively expound the sublime Dharma.

Formerly it was called Gṛdhrakūṭa-parvata; now it is called Vulture Peak Mountain (Língjiùshān). Because vultures feed on human corpses there, it is named "Vulture Peak," which has become corrupted and abbreviated.

For the sake of hearing the Dharma, King Bimbisāra mobilized his subjects to construct a stone staircase from the foot of the mountain to its peak, spanning valleys and climbing over crags. It was ten paces wide and five or six *li* in length. Along the road were two *stūpas*: the first is called "Dismounting," marking the point where the king left his carriage and proceeded on foot;
the second is called "Excluding the Vulgar," marking the point where ordinary people were screened out and not permitted to go further.

The summit of this mountain is long from east to west and narrow from south to north. On the western edge of the precipice stands a brick vihāra of extraordinary height and breadth, with its door opening toward the east; when the Tathāgata was in the world, he frequently resided here to preach the Dharma.

Now there is an image of the Buddha preaching the Dharma, equal in size to the body of the Tathāgata. To the east of the vihāra is a long stone, which is the place where the Buddha walked during his perambulations.

Beside it is a large rock, fourteen or fifteen feet high and over thirty paces in circumference; this is the one from which Devadatta hurled a stone from afar to strike the Buddha and wound his foot, causing it to bleed.
At the foot of its southern bank is a stūpa, the place where the Buddha preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Proceeding about one li from the north gate of the mountain city, one reaches the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove. To the east of the grove is a stūpa built by King Ajātaśatru as his share of the relics for worship.

Traveling five or six li southwest from the Bamboo Grove Monastery, on the northern slope of the southern mountain, there is a large stone chamber within a vast bamboo forest; this is the place where Mahākāśyapa compiled the Dharma-piṭaka.

Walking more than two hundred paces north from the Bamboo Grove Garden, one reaches the Kalandaka Pond. Two or three *li* to the northwest of the pond, one arrives at the city of Rājagṛha (translated into Chinese as "King’s Abode"). The outer walls have already crumbled, with not a single remaining section; although the inner city is ruined, its foundations still remain. It is over twenty *li* in circumference and has a single gate. Originally, King Bimbisāra resided in the upper thatched-palace city (*mārga-koṭṭa*). Because the households suffered frequent fires—where the negligence of one family brought calamity upon four neighbors—the people could not dwell in peace and the common folk lamented in resentment.
The King said:
"Because of my lack of virtue, the people have encountered this calamity; what virtuous deeds may I cultivate to dispel it?
The ministers replied:

"Great King, the common people have failed to be reverent toward your virtuous transformation; we pray that you establish strict regulations to punish future offenses. Should there be further transgressions, let them be banished to the Cold Forest (śītavana).
The Cold Forest is a place where corpses are discarded, commonly regarded as an inauspicious site."
People ceased coming and going, treating him as if he were a discarded corpse.
Since he was ashamed to remain there, he naturally became more restrained and cautious.
The king followed his advice and issued a strict edict; however, a fire subsequently broke out within the palace, causing harm.
The King said,
"I shall depart.
He then commanded the Crown Prince to oversee and manage the affairs remaining behind, while he himself moved to the Śītavana forest.

When King Vaiśālī heard that [the Buddha] was dwelling in the wilderness, he assembled an army to invade him. The frontier guards reported this to the king, who then established a city and resided there; because the king had first taken up residence here, it was called Rājagṛha (the Royal Residence).
Some say that this city was originally built prior to the succession of Ajātaśatru, who later expanded it to be higher and thicker; thus, it was not newly constructed.

When King Aśoka moved the capital to Pāṭaliputra, he bestowed Rājagṛha upon the Brāhmaṇas; consequently, there are no longer commoners within the city, which now consists entirely of Brāhmaṇas numbering some ten thousand households.
An ancient saying states:
"The Mountain City is Rājagṛha, which contains nine hundred million households;
others say that a thousand kings were established therein."
All [of these views] are erroneous.

Since the royal capital was at Rājagṛha and the Buddha resided on Vulture Peak, both the city and the mountain were manifested together to represent self and other, so that both monastics and laypeople might receive his teaching and benefit.
The treatise states:
"Regarding the accomplishment of the introductory section, this dharma-gate manifests the accomplishment of two kinds of meanings:

first, because it is the most supreme among all dharma-gates. Just as the city of Rājagṛha surpasses all other cities and dwellings—being situated at the very center of the kingdom of Magadha and serving as the capital of the king of men—it symbolizes that the One Vehicle is the Middle Way among the Three Vehicles. Since the city is superior to other cities, the sutra is superior to other sutras."

Second, it is because it manifests the accomplishment of sovereign merit. Just as Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain surpasses all other mountains, this Dharma is manifested as superior; for although Kusumā City is a mountain city and there are many mountains near Rājagṛha, this mountain alone is preeminent, lofty, and prominent. This signifies that the Dharma is high and manifest, transcending the two vehicles, and that its sovereign, majestic merit is fully perfected.
Just as a city superior to other cities has no beautiful object that does not appear within it;
just as the Dharma superior to other dharmas is not lacking in any sublime virtue;
and just as a mountain superior to other mountains is the dwelling place of beautiful birds; so too is this [the Buddha].
The Dharma excels all other dharmas because it is where superior persons dwell and roam.

Furthermore, it is said that "wondrous" (*miao*) refers to both the teaching and the principle: the teaching is wondrous as a city containing wondrous principles, and the principle is lofty as a mountain rising above the two vehicles. Thus, the fact that this sutra is located at the Royal City and Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa has its symbolic significance.
The Prajñāpāramitā permeates all five gates, yet Śrāvastī abounds in its four virtues; therefore, [the Buddha] resided there most frequently and did not rely on other locations.

It is the common tradition of the East that gold is produced in the waters of the Li River, while it is universally known in the West that the Ajitavatī River contains gold. Because birth and death (saṃsāra) are like a river that never ceases, and because nirvāṇa is like gold that may be valued as a treasure, the presence of gold within the river symbolizes the existence of perfect quiescence (parinirvāṇa) within birth and death. Thus, he preached on nirvāṇa by the banks of the Ajitavatī River.
Each has its own symbolic significance, and their origins are far-reaching.

An ancient teaching states that this sutra resides in four locations: first, on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa; second, when the stupa emerges from the midst of the air; third, when the Buddhas assemble in the Pure Land; and fourth, during the "Chapter on Entrustment," when the emanated Buddhas return to dwell in this defiled land.
Now, regarding the locations [of the teaching], it is explained that while there are three locations, they exist only in two.
As for the three locations, there is no further return to the defiled state.

In the "Entrusting" chapter at the end, the emanated bodies only then return; until the conclusion of the sutra, everything remains exclusively in the pure land. Upon returning, the land transforms back into the defiled state, and the preaching of the sutra is thus completed.
There are only two states, pure and impure:
first, when [the Buddha] was originally on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa in an impure land; second, when the Buddha transformed the land into purity as the emanated Buddhas were about to assemble.
Together with the stupa surging up into the air, there are thus three locations.

It is said that there are only two locations for its preaching: first, on Vulture Peak Mountain on earth, where he initially convened the assembly to proclaim the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) for the sake of those of the Two Vehicles and others;

and later, when the stupa emerged from the earth and the emanated Buddhas gathered in the sky, Śākyamuni sat together with Prabhūtaratna upon the same seat to encourage faith in this sutra. When the Buddha finally commanded them each to return at the conclusion of the sutra, the preaching of the scripture was finished and the Buddha returned to the ground. Since he did not preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* thereafter, we know that the places of its preaching are only these two.

Now, because this marks the inauguration of the assembly, Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa is mentioned; it marks the location where the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) dwells and acts. The Buddha speaks of the transformation body because he wishes to cause those of the three vehicles to rejoice together in it, thereby manifesting the profundity of the Buddha’s compassion and showing that both the vehicle and the body are sublime, as he is able to bestow his transformative influence even in a defiled place.

If he were to mark the reward-body (vipākakāya) Buddha or manifest a pure land, there is a fear that the assembly of those of the two vehicles would doubt that it is not their portion and thus be unable to practice; for this reason, he manifests only the defiled place and the transformation body.
The Sūtra states: "Together with a great assembly of twelve thousand bhikṣus.
The commentary says:
Among the seven accomplishments, this is the second, the accomplishment of the assembly.
The accomplishment of the assembly is explained through five gates:
first, revealing the purpose; second, manifesting the provisional and the real; third, determining the number; fourth, clarifying the sequence; and fifth, interpreting according to the treatise.
There are five reasons for [the Buddha’s] coming:
first, to provide testimony for faith.
By identifying the audience, it serves to assist in establishing that the joy of hearing the Dharma is indeed trustworthy.
There are three kinds of doubts among the assembly:
first, the doubt that Ānanda is speaking on his own authority; second, the doubt that he has heard it from others; and third, the doubt that it was spoken by someone else entirely.
Now, by demonstrating that he heard it together with [the Buddha], it is proven that the sūtra is trustworthy.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"It is spoken so as to inspire faith regarding the time, the place, and the person.
Second, it is for the purpose of manifesting [the Buddha's] virtues.

Just as Śakra, Lord of the Devas, is surrounded by the various devas, and Mahābrahmā, King of the Brahmās, is surrounded by the assembly of Brahmās, so now the Dharma King is revealed as being surrounded by the assembly of noble ones.
Third is the request for instruction.

The methods for benefiting sentient beings must correspond to their desires; they are proclaimed in sequence, first the cause and then the fruit. The body is the essence of the fruit, practice is the nature of the cause, and the vehicle (*yāna*) is that which is studied.

In the "Expedient Means" chapter (*Upāyakauśalya-parivarta*), Śāriputra’s three requests concern the provisional and ultimate aspects of the vehicles, thereby manifesting the realm of abandoning the provisional to attain the ultimate.
In the "Peaceful Practices" chapter (*Anrakugyō-parivarta*), Mañjuśrī’s earnest request correctly clarifies the practice of abandoning the provisional to attain the ultimate.

In the "Chapter on the Lifespan," Maitreya makes three requests; because this concerns the provisional and ultimate nature of his person, it reveals the fruit of relinquishing the provisional to abide in the ultimate, and as a causal scripture, it causes one to eliminate pride regarding the Dharma.

If one does not rely on a request, it is difficult for the intention [to teach] to arise; therefore, the Śrāvakas requested the realm of the One Vehicle, which perfectly accords with their faculties and leads to awakening. The Bodhisattvas, however, requested the practice and the praise of the fruit, thereby benefiting them through both the realization and the cause.
Fourth is for those who are ready to receive the teaching.

Those who have regressed from the bodhicitta gain realization through the three capacities; the One Vehicle is taught in three cycles, and when the Bodhisattvas gain realization, the teaching of the Lifespan and so forth is given, such that each receives benefit according to their kind.

Śrāvakas and ordinary beings who have distanced themselves from dust and departed from defilement give rise to the bodhicitta; those of the noble class dedicate themselves to the Mahāyāna; and ordinary bodhisattvas cast off the net of doubt, realize the truth, and attain the state of the noble ones. Since noble bodhisattvas attain the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (receptivity to the non-arising of phenomena) and shall thereby attain bodhi, this wondrous Dharma is taught for these three types of capacities.
The fifth is "attracting and gathering.

At that time, when the assembly had gathered, [the Buddha] acted to attract those present; furthermore, by recounting in detail how others in past lives generated the resolve, he aimed to inspire the intention of sentient beings in the present time, for if one lacks superior companions, pure faith will not arise.
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "The listing of bodhisattvas signifies the perfection of their retinue;
the listing of devas, nāgas, and so forth signifies the perfection of their attendants. This is true even for pure lands, let alone for defiled realms!
The five points mentioned above constitute the general purpose [of this section].
Second, it clarifies the provisional and the real.

For example, as stated in one passage of the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, within the pure and impure lands of a transformation Buddha (*nirmāṇa-buddha*), the śrāvakas and others are real, while the bodhisattvas are provisional.
In the land of recompense, bodhisattvas are the real and śrāvakas and others are provisional;
now, since both this transformation land and the land of recompense exist, there are two realities and two provisionalities according to their respective correspondences.

First, the transformation Buddhas on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa are listed; the Bodhisattvas therein represent the provisional. Sentient beings perceive the pure land as eternally peaceful at the end of the kalpa, with boundless lifespan; yet these reward bodies, reward lands, and assemblies of śrāvakas and others are not real.

Moreover, since both Prabhūtaratna and the emanated bodies are all manifested through transformation, it can be inferred that the principles of retribution, transformation, provisional, and ultimate are thereby revealed.
Since the treatise states that there are transformed śrāvakas, such as Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra and others, the remaining transformed assemblies include Prabhūtaratna, the emanated bodies, and so forth.
Regarding the number of assemblies in the three concentrations, there are fifteen assemblies in the first:

first, the assembly of highly renowned Mahāsattvas; second, the assembly of nameless Mahāsattvas; third, the assembly of respected bhikṣuṇīs; fourth, the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs from the inner retinue; fifth, the assembly of those of inconceivable holy virtue; sixth, the assembly of Śakra and the various devas; seventh, the assembly of the Three Radiant Deities and the Four Heavenly Kings; eighth, the assembly of the two Īśvaras; ninth, the assembly of the various devas of the Form Realm; tenth, the assembly of nāgas; eleventh, the assembly of kiṃnaras; twelfth, the assembly of gandharva kings; thirteenth, the assembly of asuras; fourteenth, the assembly of garuḍas; and fifteenth, the assembly of human kings.
Furthermore, there are six assemblies:
first, Many Treasures; second, the Emanated Bodies; third, the Dragon Palace; fourth, the Emergence from the Earth; fifth, Wondrous Sound; and sixth, Samantabhadra.
These two groups of followers differ in that they have heard the Dharma, realized the Dharma, practiced the Dharma, upheld the Dharma, expounded the Dharma, and protected the Dharma.
Within this, there are six distinctions regarding the gates:

first, among the three vehicles there is no separate vehicle of the pratyekabuddha; since pratyekabuddhas mostly appear separately in worlds where no Buddha exists, although the teaching is intended for them, they do not achieve the fruit at that time and thus are not present in the assembly. Nevertheless, they are fully included within the *Rènwáng jīng* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra), as the subsequent text also mentions those who seek that [vehicle].

The two realms—the desire realm and the form realm—exist, but not the formless realm. Light shines only where there are conditions for beings to come and hear the Dharma; since that [formless] realm is beyond the reach of the light and the faculties of its inhabitants are not yet mature, they do not come. This is also stated in the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*.
In the three or five destinies, there are no hells; although the light shines upon them, they do not come because they lack the necessary conditions.
There are two meanings for "coming":
first, being illuminated by the light; second, possessing the requisite conditions.
When the light of hell descends, there is no occasion for it not to reach [the being]; yet, as formlessness (*arūpya*) is entirely absent there, they do not come.
The practice of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) necessarily requires a body of leisure and opportunity; in the torments of hell, there is no leisure for such practice.
The *Dhāraṇī Sūtra* fundamentally extinguishes all suffering through its majestic power, such that even those in hell come [to hear it].
This sūtra promotes goodness; since those [in hell] have no leisure for such things, they do not come.
The reason it emits light is to cause those who see it to develop revulsion [toward saṃsāra], and to cause them, upon seeing the light, to resolve their minds so that their suffering ceases.

Regarding the fourfold assembly being without upāsakas and upāsikās, this is fully detailed in the section on the accomplishment of lower deportment; it is omitted here in the initial text for the sake of brevity.
In the fifth [section], among the eight classes of beings, there are no yakṣas or mahoragas; however, they are all present in the lower [sections].

In the sixth, among the two types of kings, there is no universal monarch (cakravartin), but only minor kings; these are also all present in the lower [sections]. These latter three are absent here, but in the subsequent explanation of the accomplishment of the majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*) as the basis, they are all enumerated in full.
Regarding the sequence of the four assemblies: first, the assembly of śrāvakas;
second, the assembly of bodhisattvas; third, the assembly of the three classes of followers; and fourth, the assembly of various kings.

Alternatively, they are ordered as internal protection followed by external protection; within internal protection, śrāvakas and bodhisattvas follow one another; among śrāvakas, monks and nuns follow one another; among monks, those with names and those without names follow one another; among nuns, those who are honored and their attendants follow one another;
and within external protection, the eight classes of beings and the kings of men follow one another.

Among the eight classes of beings, the devas (gods) and asuras (non-gods) come first; among the devas, those who dwell on earth and those who dwell in space come next; among those dwelling on earth, the sovereign and his ministers come next; and among those dwelling in space, those who are not lords of dhyāna and the lords of dhyāna come next.

As for the subsequent assemblies in sequence: the assembly that realizes the Dharma, the assembly that opens the stūpa, the assembly that extensively propagates the benefits of the sūtra, the assembly that upholds the Dharma boundlessly, the assembly that practices the Dharma in other regions, and the assembly that encourages its upholding in other regions.

Regarding why, within the initial assembly, the śrāvakas are placed first and the bodhisattvas are placed last, although this has been explained in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, I shall now provide four interpretations:
First, their physical appearances differ; the śrāvakas who have left the household life possess an appearance identical to that of the Buddhas, whereas the bodhisattvas do not.
Second, there is a distinction in proximity and distance: Śrāvakas are near to the Buddha, while Bodhisattvas are distant from him.

Third, there is a difference in the virtue of their precepts: Śrāvakas leave the household life and maintain the precepts of renunciation, whereas Bodhisattvas do not, as they manifest through transformation-births according to the various classes of beings.
The fourth intention is to cause bodhisattvas to relinquish their arrogance toward śrāvakas.

However, in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the *Rāmaka Sūtra*, the *Kṣitigarbha Sūtra*, the *Upāyakauśalya Sūtra*, and the *Sūtra on the Five Great Turbidities*, the bodhisattvas are listed first and the śrāvakas are listed later; this is because their sequence is clarified by the magnitude of their respective virtues.
Fifth, the explanation of the accomplishment of the assembly according to the treatise has four parts:
first, the number; second, the conduct; third, the inclusion of merits; and fourth, abiding in accordance with the Dharma through dignified deportment.
Regarding the accomplishment of number, it refers to the fact that the great assembly is innumerable.
While generally speaking of their being innumerable, when discussed individually they are specified as twelve thousand people and so forth.
Within the accomplishment of practice, there are four [aspects]:
First, those who are śrāvakas cultivate the practices of the Hīnayāna, sustaining themselves through alms-gathering and other such means, and are designated by names such as "bhikṣu.
Second, bodhisattvas cultivate the practices of the Mahāyāna, seeking awakening to benefit sentient beings, and are designated by the term "bodhisattva."

Third, there are bodhisattvas who, through their supernormal powers, manifest themselves according to the occasion and are able to practice the Mahāyāna. Such as the sixteen individuals including Bhadrapāla, they are fully endowed with the inconceivable deeds of a bodhisattva; because they are not fixed [in form], they are able to manifest the appearances of the four assemblies, such as upāsakas, and are thus called bodhisattvas.
The fourth point concerns the fixed deportment of renunciants, which differs from that of bodhisattvas; it is because of this fixedness that they are called *bhikṣus*.

Regarding the "accomplishment of the gathering of merits," this refers to the sixteen phrases praising the virtues of the śrāvakas and the thirteen phrases praising the virtues of the bodhisattvas, and so forth.
However, in the root treatise, these are not separately cited because the meaning of the text is already manifest.

Regarding "one who has accomplished dwelling in accordance with the rules of deportment," this refers to the passage: "At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by the fourfold assembly," and so forth.
This is because it clarifies the characteristic of the fourfold assembly surrounding the Buddha, maintaining a respectful demeanor as they listen to the Dharma.
Although each member also performs prostrations to the Buddha, this is a matter of deportment rather than the specific characteristic of listening to the Dharma; therefore, it is not mentioned here.

Within the fifteen assemblies, they are combined into three categories: Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas possess all four accomplishments; those who are in training (śaikṣa), those beyond training (aśaikṣa), and bhikṣuṇīs possess three accomplishments, as they do not extol their own virtues;
the remaining groups, such as the devas, possess two, lacking both practice and virtue.

In the treatise discussing the formation of the assembly (*parṣad*), there are four types of accomplishment mentioned in total; it does not state that each individual member must possess all four kinds.
Nevertheless, the Sūtra clarifies that within the formation of the assembly there are two sections:
first, the specific explanation of the fifteen assemblies, and second, the explanation of their dignified demeanor (*īryāpatha*).
The first part, consisting of the beginning and middle, is further divided into two sections:
first, the individual enumeration of the assembly; second, the clarification of their paying homage to the Buddha and each withdrawing to sit.
Within the fifteen groups of the assembly, there are two divisions:
First, the inner assembly of protectors is elucidated; subsequently, the outer assembly of protectors is elucidated.
Regarding the inner assembly of protectors, there are two parts:
first, the śrāvakas are elucidated; second, the bodhisattvas are elucidated.
There are two types of śrāvakas:
first, the bhikṣus are explained, and second, the bhikṣuṇīs are explained.
Within the bhikṣus, there are two [categories].
At the beginning, they were called "Highly Virtuous" (Gāude), and later they were called "Great Virtuous" (Mahāde).
Within the initial section, there are three parts:
first, designating the category and stating the number; second, praising their virtues; third, listing their names. This is the first part.
There are two accomplishments:
first, counting; second, practice.
"With" (yǔ) carries the meaning of combining, joining, together, and including.
Nāgārjuna explains:
"The same place, the same time, the same mind, the same precepts, the same views, the same path, and the same path of liberation—this is called 'shared'."

Regarding the term "Great Bhikṣu," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that there are three meanings for "great": he is the greatest among all assemblies; he has severed the great obstacles; and he is revered by great men.
Paramārtha’s threefold explanation:
First, greatness of excellence, being supreme among those in training and those beyond training.
